subject: Coffee & Tea
title: Matcha: Whisked From Stone
description: A quick win: understand Matcha: Whisked From Stone.

hook.text: Matcha is green tea ground to a powder so fine that you drink the entire leaf—not just an infusion of it.

buildup.text: Shade-grown leaves are steamed, dried, and laboriously ground on granite stone mills. One hour yields just 30 grams.

discovery.text: Because you consume the whole leaf, matcha delivers far more catechins, caffeine, and L-theanine than steeped tea.

twist.text: Ceremonial matcha costs $30–100 per 30 grams. Culinary grade (for lattes) is cheaper but far less nuanced in flavor.

climax.text: The global matcha craze turned a sacred Japanese ritual into a $4 billion industry. Tradition meets commerce.

punchline.text: Not steeped—consumed. One leaf, ground to dust, whisked to froth.

quiz.question: Why is matcha more potent than regular green tea?
options: You consume the entire powdered leaf instead of just an infusion

details.summary: Matcha is made by stone-grinding shade-grown tea leaves into a fine powder that is whisked with hot water. The stone milling process is slow, producing only about 40 grams per hour per mill.
details.whyItMatters: Stone milling is what makes matcha special. The slow, low-heat process prevents oxidation and preserves the delicate compounds that give matcha its unique character.
takeaways: Matcha is stone-ground from shade-grown tea leaves
Stone mills produce only about 40 grams per hour
Slow grinding preserves flavor, color, and nutrients

faq.question: Why is real matcha so expensive?
faq.answer: The shade-growing period reduces yield, hand-picking selects only the finest leaves, stems and veins are removed before grinding, and stone milling is extremely slow. A single granite mill produces about 40 grams of powder per hour. Each step adds labor and cost to the final product.

faq.question: How can you tell quality matcha from cheap powder?
faq.answer: Quality matcha is vivid bright green, smells fresh and grassy, and tastes smooth with umami sweetness. Low-quality matcha is yellowish or dull green, smells stale, and tastes bitter. Price is usually a reliable indicator. Ceremonial grade from reputable Japanese producers is the safest choice.
